what_its_for: Levorphanol is a strong opioid pain medicine used to treat moderate to severe pain that is not well controlled by other pain medicines. It belongs to the same family as morphine and works by changing how your brain and body feel pain.
how_to_take: Take levorphanol exactly as your doctor prescribed. You can take it with or without food, but if it upsets your stomach, taking it with food or milk may help. Swallow the tablet whole — do not crush, chew, or break it. Never take more than your prescribed dose or take it more often than directed. This is a powerful medication, so it is very important to follow your doctor's instructions carefully.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on the lowest dose that controls your pain and may slowly increase it if needed. A typical starting dose for adults is 2 mg taken every 6 to 8 hours, but your dose may be different based on your pain level, other medicines you take, and your overall health. Always use the dose your doctor has prescribed for you — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next scheduled dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one, as this could lead to a dangerous overdose.
storage: Store levorphanol at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Store it in a secure, locked place out of reach of children and pets. Never share this medication with anyone else — sharing opioids is dangerous and illegal. If you have unused or expired tablets, dispose of them safely using a drug take-back program or a medication disposal kiosk near you.
what_to_avoid: Do not drink alcohol while taking levorphanol — combining them can cause dangerous breathing problems or even death. Avoid taking other medicines that make you sleepy, such as sleeping pills, anti-anxiety medicines, muscle relaxers, or other opioids, unless your doctor says it is okay. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do anything that requires you to be fully alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid suddenly stopping this medicine without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: slow, shallow, or stopped breathing; extreme sleepiness or you cannot be woken up; severe dizziness or fainting; confusion or unusual behavior; chest pain or fast or irregular heartbeat; severe constipation or stomach pain; or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, or swelling of the face, lips, or throat. If you or someone else has taken too much levorphanol, call 911 or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) immediately and use naloxone (Narcan) if it is available.
when_it_works: Levorphanol usually begins to relieve pain within 30 to 60 minutes after you take it. Because it stays in your body longer than some other opioids, it can build up over time, so your doctor will monitor you carefully, especially in the first few days. It is important to take it on a consistent schedule as directed to keep your pain under control.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and older): You may be more sensitive to the effects of levorphanol, including dizziness, confusion, and breathing problems. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose. Pregnancy: Levorphanol can harm an unborn baby and may cause the baby to be born dependent on opioids (neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome). Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Levorphanol can pass into breast milk and harm a nursing baby. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney or liver problems: These conditions can cause the medicine to build up in your body to unsafe levels. Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely.
